kurz: How the purchase price, interest rate and repayment rate turn into an instalment, a term and an outstanding balance, and which of these variables the borrower can control.

bloecke.md:
When you buy a property with a loan, you sign a loan agreement running for several decades in addition to the purchase contract. The property is often chosen over months, whereas the loan agreement is frequently signed in an afternoon. Yet clearer rules apply to the loan agreement, and it offers more scope for influencing the costs.

All the calculations in this lesson relate to the same case. The property costs €400,000 and is located in North Rhine-Westphalia. On top of this come 6.5% real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer), around 1.5% for the notary and land register and a halved estate agent's commission of 3.57%. The incidental costs thus total 11.57% or €46,280, and the total outlay €446,280. Of this, €96,280 is paid from equity, and the loan amounts to €350,000. The borrowing rate (Sollzins) is 3.90% nominal. With monthly payments, this results in an effective interest rate of 3.97%. This is the figure that Dr. Klein (a German mortgage broker) published on 3 September 2026 for a ten-year fixed-rate period.

bloecke.formel:
Instalment = S0 × ((1 + i)^n × i) / ((1 + i)^n − 1)
Outstanding balance_k = S0 × (1 + i)^k − Instalment × ((1 + i)^k − 1) / i
bloecke.erklaerung: The annuity loan has a constant instalment, which can be calculated with the first line. The second line gives the outstanding balance after k periods, that is, the amount still owed at the end of the fixed-rate period. Because banks calculate monthly, i is the monthly interest rate and n the number of months. Since interest is charged more than once a year, the effective interest rate is always above the borrowing rate.
variablen: number of periods until full repayment
bloecke.beispiel: €350,000 at a 3.90% borrowing rate with a 2% initial repayment rate: Instalment = 350,000 × 5.9% / 12 = €1,720.83 a month.

bloecke.md:
## Initial repayment rate and composition of the instalment

In practice, the instalment is not calculated from the term n. Instead, an **initial repayment rate** is agreed, typically 2% to 3%. Together with the borrowing rate, it gives the annual annuity as a percentage of the loan amount. In this way, 3.90% plus 2.00% becomes 5.90% of €350,000, that is, €20,650 a year or €1,720.83 a month.

The instalment stays the same, but its composition changes. In the first year, €13,524 goes to the bank as interest and only €7,126 into repayment. In the tenth year, it is €10,533 interest and €10,117 repayment. The repayment portion rises each year by roughly the percentage of the borrowing rate, because from then on no more interest is charged on each euro repaid. This is the same compound interest effect as with saving, except that here it lowers interest costs instead of increasing income.

Effect of a higher initial repayment rate
bloecke.md: An initial repayment rate of 3% instead of 2% costs €291.67 more a month. In return, the financing ends 6.4 years earlier, and the total interest burden falls by around €57,000. A low instalment therefore extends the period in which interest is charged and increases the total cost.

## Fixed-rate period and interest rate premium

The interest rate is only guaranteed for the agreed **fixed-rate period** (Sollzinsbindung). After that, the market rate then prevailing applies to the outstanding balance. A longer fixed-rate period costs a premium. On 3 September 2026, effective interest rates were 3.93% for five years, 3.97% for ten, 4.17% for fifteen, 4.30% for twenty and 4.48% for thirty years.

This premium turns out smaller than it first appears. Switching from a ten-year to a fifteen-year fixed-rate period increases the monthly instalment by €55.42 with the same initial repayment rate, which comes to around €6,650 over ten years. In return, the interest rate is fixed for five years longer, and the outstanding balance at the end of the fixed-rate period falls from €264,556 to €205,386. This decrease comes almost entirely from the five additional years of repayment. After ten years, the outstanding balance with the higher instalment is around €263,700, only around €860 below the figure with a ten-year fixed-rate period.

bloecke.titel: Right of termination after ten years
bloecke.md: Under Section 489(1) no. 2 BGB (Civil Code), the borrower may terminate the loan ten years after receiving it in full, giving six months' notice, regardless of a longer fixed-rate period and without an early repayment charge. This right cannot be excluded by contract. In economic terms, a fixed-rate period of more than ten years therefore works like an option. If interest rates rise, the old rate continues to apply; if they fall, the borrower can get out after the tenth year. The premium of around 0.2 to 0.5 percentage points is the price of this option.

## Loan-to-value ratio and equity

The **loan-to-value ratio** (Beleihungsauslauf) relates the loan amount to the mortgage lending value, not to the purchase price. The bank estimates the mortgage lending value cautiously; a discount of around 10% on the purchase price is usual. In addition, incidental purchase costs do not increase the mortgage lending value at all. Anyone who finances them as well is therefore borrowing money that is not backed by any collateral.

Banks grade their terms according to the loan-to-value ratio, usually in tiers around 60%, 80% and 100%. The size of the premium for each tier is not reliably published anywhere; it depends on the bank, the borrower's creditworthiness and the property. The order of magnitude can be calculated, however.

bloecke.titel: Three equity ratios for the same property (purchase price €400,000, incidental costs €46,280)

bloecke.md:
Illustrative calculation for €350,000 and ten years with a constant instalment of €1,720.83.

- At a 3.90% borrowing rate, the outstanding balance after ten years is €264,556 and the interest paid €121,056.
- At 4.20%, the outstanding balance is €276,213 and the interest €132,713.
- At 4.50%, the outstanding balance is €288,261 and the interest €144,761.

Each premium of 0.3 percentage points costs around €11,700 to €12,000 over ten years, with the same instalment entirely at the expense of repayment. An additional €40,000 of equity that moves the financing into a more favourable pricing tier often earns more than an investment in the capital market.

If real estate transfer tax, notary and estate agent are financed as well, the financing in the example starts at a loan-to-value ratio of 124%. The bank charges a significant premium for this, and in the first years the loan is not covered by the property. In a forced sale, debts then remain. The incidental purchase costs therefore do not belong in the loan; they determine the minimum equity required.

## Special repayment, full-repayment loan and KfW funding

A **special repayment right** costs nothing at most banks if it is requested before the contract is signed. Up to 5% of the original loan amount per year is usual. Without a contractual commitment, early repayment during the fixed-rate period outside Section 489 BGB is only possible if there is a legitimate interest and against an early repayment charge (Section 490(2), Section 500(2) BGB). If the borrower in the example repays an extra €3,000 every year, the outstanding balance after ten years falls from €264,556 to €228,587. The term shortens from 27.8 to 22.2 years, and the borrower saves around €49,000 in interest.

With a **full-repayment loan** (Volltilgerdarlehen), the fixed-rate period matches the term. No outstanding balance remains at the end, and there is no follow-up financing risk. In return, the instalment is high. With full repayment in ten years, the example loan costs €3,526.97 a month, which corresponds to an initial repayment rate of 8.19%; over fifteen years, it is €2,604.72. The total interest burden thus falls to €73,236 and €118,850 respectively, compared with €223,733 in the standard case with slow repayment. Full-repayment loans usually have a slightly more favourable interest rate, but the instalment cannot be reduced later.

**KfW** (the German state-owned development bank) only supports property purchases in certain cases. Programme 300 *Home ownership for families* (Wohneigentum für Familien) requires at least one child under 18, no other residential property in Germany, owner occupation and a taxable household income of at most €90,000, plus €10,000 for each additional child. The loan amount ranges from €170,000 to €270,000 depending on the number of children and the efficiency standard, with a term of up to 35 years. Programme 124 is open to all owner-occupiers with up to €100,000, and programmes 297/298 support climate-friendly new builds with up to €150,000. KfW interest rates change at short notice and are therefore not quantified here. They should be looked up on the day of the decision and compared with the bank's offer, including all ancillary conditions and not just the interest rate.

## Repaying or investing

For owner-occupied properties, interest on debt is not tax-deductible. Every euro repaid therefore earns a risk-free and tax-free return equal to the borrowing rate, here 3.90%. An investment must achieve this figure after tax. Gains from an equity fund are subject to 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, together 26.375% (Section 32d(1) EStG, Income Tax Act). The 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) reduces the effective burden to 18.4625%. An equity ETF would therefore have to earn around 4.78% before tax to draw level, and do so without risk, which it cannot deliver. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person (Section 20(9) EStG) lowers this threshold only for small amounts invested.

For let properties, the trade-off is reversed, because interest on debt counts as income-related expenses (Werbungskosten) there; this is covered in the tax lesson of this module. In addition, there should be an emergency fund before any special repayment. Money that has gone into repayment is no longer available, and in an emergency the bank will not lend it back at the same interest rate.

## End of the fixed-rate period

At the end of the fixed-rate period, there are three options. **Renewal** (Prolongation) is the follow-up offer from the existing bank. It is convenient and requires neither a notary nor a new credit check, but it is rarely the best offer on the market. When **refinancing** with another bank, the land charge (Grundschuld) must be assigned, which incurs notary fees. With a significant outstanding balance, refinancing is nevertheless usually cheaper. Under Section 493(1) BGB, the bank must state at the latest three months before the end of the fixed-rate period whether it is prepared to agree a new interest rate at all. That is the latest date; you should start comparing offers much earlier.

The third option is the **forward mortgage** (Forward-Darlehen), in which the follow-up interest rate is fixed up to 60 months in advance. For this, the bank charges a forward premium on the current interest rate, which rises with the lead time. In 2015, Stiftung Warentest (the German consumer testing organisation) found around 0.58 percentage points for a three-year lead time. The figure shows the order of magnitude, but it is not a price for 2026. Two conditions must be observed. There is an **obligation to draw down** the loan, and anyone who does not draw it down pays a non-acceptance fee (Nichtabnahmeentschädigung). In addition, you no longer benefit from falling interest rates. A forward mortgage therefore serves as a hedge against rising interest rates, not as speculation on them.

bloecke.unter: The lead time before the end of the fixed-rate period offers the greatest room for manoeuvre; on the day the fixed-rate period ends, only the current market conditions apply.

bloecke.md: Under Section 500(2) BGB, a consumer mortgage loan (Immobiliar-Verbraucherdarlehen) can only be repaid early during the fixed-rate period if there is a legitimate interest, typically when the property is sold. The bank may charge an early repayment charge for this, which it calculates on the basis of its interest loss (Section 502 BGB). The percentage cap that applies to general consumer loans does not apply here. With a high outstanding balance and a long remaining fixed-rate period, five-figure amounts can therefore add up. Anyone who considers a move during the fixed-rate period possible should secure the necessary flexibility from the outset, for example through a shorter fixed-rate period or generous special repayment rights.

- Borrowing rate and effective interest rate, both for the same fixed-rate period
- Initial repayment rate as a percentage, not just the monthly instalment
- Outstanding balance at the end of the fixed-rate period, stated in euros
- Special repayment right with the amount per year and whether it is free of charge, lapses if unused or can be accumulated
- Right to change the repayment rate during the term, ideally more than once
- Commitment interest with start date and amount (important for new builds)
- Mortgage lending value applied, because it determines the pricing tier

mitnehmen: The monthly instalment is not suitable for comparing loan offers; what can be compared are the effective interest rate, the initial repayment rate and the outstanding balance at the end of the fixed-rate period, stated in euros.
In the example, one percentage point more initial repayment costs €291.67 a month, saves around €57,000 in interest and shortens the term by 6.4 years.
Incidental purchase costs do not increase the mortgage lending value; they do not belong in the loan and determine the minimum amount of equity needed.
Under Section 489(1) no. 2 BGB, every loan can be terminated after ten years, so that from then on a longer fixed-rate period only works in the borrower's favour.
For an owner-occupied home, repayment brings a tax-free and safe return equal to the borrowing rate; to match it, an investment would have to earn around 4.8% before tax, and just as safely.

begriffe.text: Constant annual or monthly instalment made up of interest and repayment. Its amount stays the same, but with each instalment the share shifts from interest to repayment.
Repayment portion in the first year as a percentage of the loan amount. Together with the borrowing rate, it gives the annuity, for example 3.90% plus 2.00% equals 5.90% of the loan amount per year.

Loan amount divided by the mortgage lending value, which the bank sets cautiously below the purchase price. The loan-to-value ratio determines the pricing tier. Incidental purchase costs financed with the loan increase it without adding any collateral.
Loan whose fixed-rate period matches its term. No outstanding balance remains at the end, but the instalment is high and a later change in the repayment rate is usually ruled out.

Follow-up loan whose interest rate is fixed up to 60 months in advance. The bank charges a forward premium for this. There is an obligation to draw down the loan, and the borrower does not benefit from falling interest rates.
